Animals Female BALB/c mice (6-8 weeks old) were obtained from SPF Biotechnology Co., LTD (Beijing, China). Mice were randomly grouped and each 6 mice were housed in one cage in SPF conditions under a 12h light/12h dark cycle with free access to food and water. For experimental colitis mouse model, mice received four 7-day cycles of 3% DSS in drinking water, each followed by three 14-day cycles of normal drinking water, according to a previous study with some modifications ( ). For Bifidobacterium intervention experiments, after 1 week of adaptive feeding, mice in the Bifidobacterium group received an oral gavage with 2×10 8 CFU/200 μL Bifidobacterium for two consecutive weeks, while mice in the control group were received saline buffer. Two Bifidobacterium including Bifidobacterium longum subsp. infantis (SHBCC D11206 AS1.1853) and Bifidobacterium adolescentis (SHBCC D11107 ) were selected for the present study, and both of them were purchased from ZHONGKE-JIAYI (Shandong, China) and maintained in our laboratory. For antibiotic treatment experiments, antibiotic cocktail was prepared to eliminate the initial gut microbiota according to the previous study ( ). Mice received an oral gavage with 1 mg/kg amphotericin-B for three consecutive days, and then each mouse was given an antibiotic cocktail of 100 mg/kg neomycin trisulfate, 50 mg/kg vancomycin, 100 mg/kg metronidazole and 1 mg/kg amphotericin-B for seven consecutive days. Ampicillin was dissolved into drinking water at a concentration 1 g/L for mice. All antibiotics were purchased from Macklin Biochemical Technology (Shanghai, China) and Solarbio Life Science (Beijing, China). After antibiotic treatment, the mice received Bifidobacterium intervention according the methods mentioned above. Our present study employed three models, including the DSS-induced colitis model, germ-free mouse model, and the in vitro human intestinal γδ T cell co-culture model, to systematically assess the effects of Bifidobacteria derived from different age groups. We investigated changes in gut microbial composition and abundance, intestinal transcriptomic features, and alterations in relevant immune cell subsets and their functions following Bifidobacterial intervention. Our results revealed significant differences in how Bifidobacteria from various age groups, specifically strains BA and BI, rebuild gut microbiota ecosystem and activate immune-related signaling pathways, both within the same model and across different models. In both in vivo models, short-term continuous probiotic interventions did not restore gut microbial levels and diversity to normal. In the DSS-induced colitis model, DSS treatment led to a shortening of the colorectal length, and short-term interventions with either Bifidobacteria strain failed to return it to normal levels. Transcriptomic data from the DSS-induced model identified γδ T cells as key responders, with significant activation of γ-chain utilizing genes. Although DSS is the primary agent for inducing colitis, it does not directly affect bacteria ( ), suggesting that DSS primarily influences the gut microbial environment indirectly by affecting the intestinal immune milieu. Analysis of transcriptomic data indicated that Bifidobacteria from different age groups differentially impacted gut immunity and microbial diversity. In-depth studies of probiotics from various age groups could facilitate more precise treatments for intestinal inflammations, such as IBD across different age demographics. The effects of single or multiple probiotic strains on intestinal microbial diversity and immunity may depend on the specific intestinal environment of the host from which they were originally isolated. When using mixed probiotic preparations, it is essential to consider the competition and coordination between microorganisms. Additionally, microbial interventions should account for potential incompatibilities, similar to drug interactions. The role of TLR and NLR signaling pathways in food allergies, chronic intestinal diseases and autoimmune conditions has been studied ( ; ). BA exhibited minimal direct effects on γδ T cells, suggesting that its immunomodulatory role might be mediated indirectly, potentially through other immune cells or via modifications of the local cytokine milieu. chunks.content: Introduction Cardiac computed tomography has become a mainstay in the noninvasive diagnosis and assessment of coronary heart disease. Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) is recommended for initial testing of patients suspected of having obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD) and may reduce the need for invasive coronary angiography (ICA) [ ]. Adding CCTA to routine testing has been shown to lower the rate of a combined endpoint of cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction [2]. Initial CCTA instead of ICA has a similar risk of major adverse cardiovascular events, but a lower rate of major procedure-related complications [ ]. However, CCTA is not recommended for patients with irregular heart rates or other conditions that may lead to lower image quality [ ]. CCTA can be performed using different scan modes, with mode choice depending on heart rate and heart rate variability. Premedication with nitrates or beta-blockers can improve image quality significantly [ ]. The lowest radiation dose is generally obtained by using the high-pitch mode, which has been made possible by the introduction of dual-source CT scanners and termed FLASH mode [ , ]. By performing a single ECG-synchronized high-pitch scan of the whole heart radiation exposure is kept minimal. FLASH-mode CCTA can be performed if three requirements are met: the patient has both a low heart rate and a regular heart rhythm, as well as a high temporal resolution of the CT scanner. If these requirements are not met, the sequential scan mode is chosen, which demonstrates higher signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) but much higher dose exposures [ ]. That thresholds for heart rate or heart rate variability above FLASH-mode scanning become inadvisable has been the subject of considerable research interest, with a broad range of found values [ – ]. A possible explanation are differences in scanner design and scanning parameters, as even third-generation CT scanners demonstrated higher SNR in FLASH mode than second-generation devices. Recently, photon-counting detector computed tomography (PCCT) scanners have been introduced into clinical practice. The differences in detector design and resulting advantages over conventional energy-integrating detectors (EID) have been described in detail elsewhere [ , ]. They can briefly be summarized as photon-counting detectors (PCD) having a higher inherent spatial resolution and photon efficiency, which can be used either to increase image quality or reduce radiation dose. It is, therefore, necessary to reevaluate under which conditions FLASH-mode CCTA can be performed using PCCT scanners and how to optimize image quality and dose exposure. Herein, we investigated the influence of heart rate and heart rate variability on image quality and motion artifacts scores of FLASH-mode CCTA. Both HR and HRV were significantly associated with the presence of motion artifacts (both p < 0.001) in a combined model. We chose to define heart rate variability in terms of the standard deviation of the five heartbeats preceding the acquisition of the CT angiography. This is equivalent to the commonly applied standard deviation of the normal R-R intervals (SDNN). We obtained a mean SDNN of 55.2 ± 68.1 ms, which is in line with previous studies in patients with compromised cardiac health [ , ]. The influence of HRV on both diagnostic quality and motion artifact scores is plausible from a mechanistic point of view. Variations in the R-R intervals prior to the scan lead to mistiming of the acquisition, which then falls, instead of the ideal mid-diastole, in intervals of the heart cycle with increased cardiac wall movement. Elevated HR itself does not inherently lead to mistimed acquisitions but shortens the ideal time interval. Accordingly, while the HR is a significant predictor of the motion artifact score, the correlation coefficient is very low (Pearson’s correlation coefficient 0.10). At the same dose, the higher photon efficiency leads to lower image noise [ ], possibly shifting the threshold above which unacceptable decreases in image quality occur. Furthermore, the generated virtual monoenergetic images improve iodine contrast, which may allow better differentiation between cardiac vessels and tissue [ ]. Only 5.4% of the included patients had a HR of 70 or more, and the highest recorded heart rate at the scan was 73. Therefore, further studies including patients with higher HR are indicated. A recent study demonstrated FLASH-mode scanning is possible for the majority of pediatric patients with heart rates < 100 bpm with adequate proximal coronary visualization [ ]. In another study, average HR and HRV were significantly higher in patients with at least one nondiagnostic segment, and all patients with HR < 64 bpm and HRV < 13 bpm, as defined by the difference between the maximum and minimum HR, had diagnostic image quality in all segments [ ]. Another study found that HR and motion artifacts on the preceding coronary artery calcium quantification scan are independent predictors of image quality [ ]. In a combined phantom-patient study, distortion of coronary arteries was less than 1 mm for HR up to 75 bpm in the phantom and the depiction of patient coronary segments was of diagnostic image quality for all patients with HR up to 73 bpm [ ]. The main limiting factor is the retrospective nature and the restriction on the analysis of patients who received only FLASH scans. As the choice of scan mode was left to the performing physician, patients with significant arrhythmia or elevated heart rates were naturally excluded, leading to significant selection bias. However, as no fixed threshold was set beforehand, borderline cases were indeed included, as can be seen in the relatively high number of patients with HR for which normally a different scan mode would be chosen. Additionally, possible changes in HR and HRV between the timepoint of mode selection and the scan would inherently fuzzy such a threshold. Another factor is the inherent subjectivity of image quality and motion artifact scoring. While the scores were determined in consensus, a study with multiple readers would possibly reduce reading bias. Minor limiting factors were the relatively low patient number, possible temporal changes in heart rhythm due to the different amount of administered premedication, and the inclusion of patients both with and without known coronary, structural or functional heart disease. Furthermore, we did not perform a direct comparison between cardiac CTs performed on either EID-CT or PCCT scanners, which would provide further information on possible differences in the HR threshold. This preliminary study represents the first investigation regarding the possible selection of scan mode in photon-counting cardiac CT imaging. Due to the retrospective and preliminary nature, changes in mode selection or threshold values can and should not be drawn. Further investigations with possible randomization or comparison between scan modes and inclusion of patients with higher heart rates are urgently necessary to improve the strength of evidence and provide clinical guidelines. Conclusion We could demonstrate that the scan heart rate variability, but not the mean heart rate during FLASH-mode PCCT coronary angiography is significantly associated with reduced subjective diagnostic quality and increased motion artifacts in a preliminary study with a maximum HR of 73 bpm and maximum HRV of 37 bpm. This has implications for the selection of scan mode choice and subsequently possibly reductions in mean applied radiation dose. The results are in line with previous results investigating last-generation conventional energy-integrating CT, and it is possible that PCCT scanners may push the HR threshold above which motion artifacts begin influencing image quality even higher.

chunks.content: Introduction Managing children with syndromes associated with an increased risk of malignancies poses a complex challenge for healthcare providers. These syndromes, often rare and diverse, were the focus of discussion at the 2023 AACR Childhood Cancer Predisposition Workshop. Herein, we summarize the clinical and genetic aspects of select cancer predisposition syndromes (CPS), including enchondromatoses (Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome), hereditary multiple osteochondromas and related syndromes, hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma syndrome (HLRCC), Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome and Schinzel-Giedion syndrome. Several of these syndromes were discussed at the 2016 AACR Predisposition Workshop( , ) and were reviewed again in light of contemporary literature, updating recommendations where appropriate. Other syndromes, including of enchondromas and osteochondromas, were not discussed in the 2016 Workshop. All of these syndromes are associated with elevated childhood cancer risk but differ with respect to specific risks, molecular etiology and phenotypic manifestations. For each, the expert panel reviewed whether sufficient data exists to make a recommendation for cancer surveillance during childhood. Decision-making was based on the incidence of malignancies, ages of highest risk, the importance of early detection of specific tumors in terms of impact on outcome, the benefits and risks of the different surveillance modalities, considering any relevant co-existing morbidities. For all syndromes, the panel recommends increased awareness and prompt assessment of clinical symptoms. A summary of these recommendations is presented in and Enchondromatoses (Multiple Enchondromas Syndromes) - Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome Enchondromas are benign cartilaginous neoplasms that arise from the medullary cavity of bones and cause bone expansion. They typically grow to sizes up to 3 cm and do not cause pain( ). Enchondromatoses refers to a group of rare diseases with multiple enchondromas. The most common is Ollier disease (OD, OMIM #166000), with prevalence estimates of 1:100,000, which usually presents with enchondromas in early life (median age 4.8–11y)( ). The enchondromas are often found in the short and long tubular bones of the limbs but can involve the axial skeleton (pelvis, ribs) and can be unilateral or bilateral( ). In Maffucci syndrome (MS, OMIM #614569), these characteristics are accompanied by a propensity for benign vascular overgrowths, which can be cutaneous, visceral, or occur in soft tissues. In contrast to most other CPS described in the AACR series, these conditions typically arise from a post-zygotic pathogenic variant (PV) in the lesion, causing somatic mosaicism rather than a constitutional alternation: in 80%, there are somatic variants in IDH1 (at p.Arg132) or IDH2 (p.Arg172Ser)( , ). Germline PVs in PTHR1 ( – ) and germline or early post-zygotic PVs in HIF1A, VHL, IDH1 , and other genes related to the HIF-1 pathway are also reported, although these findings require further validation( ). Thus, while diagnosis is based on clinical findings, when assessing individuals it is important to consider alternate diagnoses, such as hereditary multiple osteochondromas (discussed below), metachondromatosis (OMIM # 156250), spondyloenchondrodysplasia with immune dysregulation (OMIM #607944), spondylomegaepiphyseal-metaphyseal dysplasia (OMIM # 609616 ), and metaphyseal enchondromatosis with D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (OMIM # 614875 ). Malignant transformation of the enchondromas to chondrosarcoma is notable, occurring in about 30% of patients( , – ). It can happen in any bone, and the sites with the highest rates include the femur, tibia, humerus, pelvis and scapula( , , , ). Transformations occur at a median age of 30–52 years, but can occur as young as 10 years( , ). Local pain is typical but not uniform, as there are several reports of asymptomatic chondrosarcomas, and conversely there are some reports of pain in the setting of benign lesions. Increasing tumor size may also suggest transformation. Nevertheless, the prognosis of patients with secondary chondrosarcomas is generally good, with 5-year survival of over 90%, since the grade of the sarcoma is often low and the tumors rarely metastasize( , ). In MS, 8.5% of vascular lesions undergo malignant transformation( ). Interestingly, other malignancies are also prevalent; in OD and possibly MS, gliomas were reported in 1.2–16.3% of patients( , , ), and most harbor somatic mutations in either IDH1 or IDH2 genes( , ). Reported tumors were morphologically diffuse low-grade gliomas or anaplastic astrocytomas, usually diagnosed at younger ages than sporadic cases and can present with multi-focal disease( , ). Juvenile granulosa cell tumors were reported in at least twelve cases( , – ), some with molecular data showing the same IDH variant as in the enchondromas. Patients are also at risk of other cancers, but surprisingly, despite IDH1/2 presenting as recurring variants in sporadic leukemia, leukemia has been only rarely reported in patients with OD or MS( ). Other complications of enchondromatoses include limb deformities, bone shortening with leg length discrepancy, limitations in joint mobility, scoliosis, gait disturbances, pain and pathological fractures( ). Our consortium acknowledges that while the higher risk of malignancy may be due to ascertainment bias( ), it is likely high enough to warrant surveillance. Studies of the optimal methods and intervals of surveillance are needed. Additionally, with the availability of targeted inhibitors against IDH1 and/or IDH2 , the impact of early diagnosis and such novel therapies may need to be systematically studied and revisited in the future( ). With these caveats, we recommend that patients should undergo a baseline whole-body MRI (WBMRI) for assessment of bone lesions and vascular anomlies, and osseous deformities may also be evident. Targeted magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) should be added for vascular anomalies when detected, at the same time or at follow-up. The baseline MRI should be deferred to avoid the need for general anesthesia at the time of the diagnosis, typically until 6–8 years of age, and if there are no concerning symptoms or enchondromas. Bone scintigraphy can be considered where WBMRI is unavailable, with focused radiographs of every enchondroma. A thorough physical examination, which includes musculoskeletal and neurological assessment, should be undertaken every 6–12 months until adulthood (12–24 months in adulthood), with plain radiographs of the known lesions at least every 2–3 years, depending on the enchondroma location. For children, a yearly dedicated MRI should be considered for lesions larger than 5–6 cm or lesions located in the pelvis or scapula, even if asymptomatic. Although very rare in children, given the good outcomes with early intervention/management options for gliomas, some centers also suggest a dedicated brain MRI with contrast at early adolescence for detection of asymptomatic gliomas. From 20 years, WBMRI should be offered every one to two years and should include a high-quality dedicated brain MRI. Further work-up, including targeted MRI and biopsy, is warranted in case of new pain or radiological findings suspecting transformation. In addition, due to the high incidence of other malignancies, a high index of suspicion should be employed for other symptoms at any age, including neurological symptoms (glioma), lower abdominal pain in women (juvenile granulosa cell tumor), and constitutional signs. Hereditary Multiple Osteochondromas (HMO) Osteochondromas are cartilage-covered neoplasms that arise from the surface of bone. Hereditary Multiple Osteochondromas (HMO)( ) is a rare genetic disorder associated with the development of osteochondromas in the metaphysis of long bones and the surface of flat bones. Several other terms have been used including hereditary multiple exostoses, hereditary deforming chondrodysplasia, multiple cartilaginous exostoses, diaphyseal aclasis, and Bessel Hagen disease( – ). HMO is primarily caused by PVs in one of two tumor suppressor genes. EXT1 (Exostosin Glycosyltransferase 1, OMIM 608177, chr 8q24.11) accounts for approximately 65–70% of cases, and EXT2 ( OMIM 608210, chr 11p11.2) for 30–35%. In the majority of individuals, there is a positive family history of disease, although approximately 10% of individuals are de novo ( – ). EXT3 ( OMIM 600209) has been also suggested as causative, though the exact gene on chromosome 19 has not been identified( , ). The cause is still unknown in about 10% of cases( , – ). The prevalence of HMO is estimated to be 1/50,000 in North America but is highly variable depending on geographic locations, from 1/100,000 in the United Kingdom to 1/1,000 in Guam ( , , , ). Penetrance is estimated to be near 100% in males and 96% in females( , , ). By the time growth plates fuse at the end of puberty, many patients have osteochondromas throughout their skeleton( , ). Individuals may present with reports of pain, short stature, angular deformities of long bones, scoliosis, and leg length discrepancy( , , ). Malignant transformation into chondrosarcoma occurs in 0.2–5.9% of individuals( , , , , , ). Of those who develop chondrosarcoma, 75% are between 20 and 40 years of age, but earlier occurrences are reported. In one study, 7% of secondary chondrosarcomas occurred in individuals younger than 20 years, with the youngest at 13 years( ), and there is a report of malignancy occurring as early as 9 years of age( ). Incidence of transformation is higher in males and individuals with an EXT1 PV, and more common in the pelvis, scapula, femur, and humerus( , , , , , ). Evidence of rapid growth of an osteochondroma, increasing pain and/or a bulky cartilage cap that is thicker than 2.0 to 3.0 cm on an MRI or CT scan suggest progression to chondrosarcoma( , ). There is a tendency for osteochondromas to enlarge until skeletal maturity, and there are additional non-cancerous risks, including bony deformities and cord compression (in the case of vertebral lesions). Thus, as noted in previous studies, we recommend annual physical examinations starting in childhood( ) with early investigations in case of increasing pain or rapid growth of lesions. We also recommend considering a baseline skeletal survey at early adolescence (around 12 years), when most osteochondromas have evolved and before the age of transformation risk. This should be done preferably by WBMRI or plain radiographs if the former is not available. Fei et al.( ) suggested that annual MRI screening for all patients with HMO may be valuable between the ages of 20 and 40, but in childhood, there is currently not enough data to advocate for routine surveillance. We endorse the recommendation to consider regular regional MRI (every 2–3 years) of osteochondromas identified in the pelvis or scapula( , ), as transformation is more common in these locations, particularly in males or EXT1 PV carriers. In contrast to enchondromas (see above), due to the high burden on osteochondromas and the considerably low frequency of malignant transformation, we do not recommend regular plain films of all known lesions. Orthopedic providers should preferably be involved in the monitoring of osteochondromas. Two contiguous gene deletion syndromes which include either EXT1 or 2 are Potocki-Shaffer Syndrome (PSS) and Tricho-rhino-phalangeal II (TRPS II). PSS is a condition caused by a heterozygous deletion at chromosome 11p12-p11.2, resulting in haploinsufficiency of the genes EXT2 , ALX4 and PHF21A . With just over 30 patients reported in the literature, clinical features of the syndrome include minor craniofacial abnormalities, biparietal foramina, developmental delay, intellectual disability, genitourinary anomalies, and multiple exostoses( – ). There are as yet no reports of patients with PSS developing sarcomatous transformation in this small cohort of individuals. TRPS II, also referred to as Langer-Giedion syndrome, is caused by the contiguous gene deletion of TRPS1 , RAD21 , and EXT1 on chromosome 8( ). Clinical features include a bulbous nose with a broad nasal bridge, fine, sparse, slow-growing hair, dystrophic nails and skeletal findings. This condition is associated with the development of multiple osteochondromas, usually first observed on the scapulae, around the elbows and knees, and an increased risk for intellectual disability( ). There are few reports of secondary chondrosarcoma in TRPS II as well as two cases of primary osteosarcoma arising distant from an osteochondroma in one family( , ). However, in a large study of 103 individuals with TRPS (including mostly type I, which do not involve deletions of EXT 1), there were no cases of bone malignancy( ). The specific risk for malignancy is therefore unknown. Thus, for both PSS and TRPS II, based on the molecular loss of function of EXT1/ EXT2 , the rarity of the syndromes and the unknown potential for malignant degeneration of osteochondromas, surveillance in a similar manner to individuals with HMO can be suggested but is not strongly recommended. Nevertheless, when symptomatic, it is recommended to perform imaging of osteochondromas, preferably by dedicated MRI. Care should preferably be taken in an academic center, with expertise in rare syndromes or syndromes of bone lesions. Fibrodysplasia Ossificans Progressiva Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is characterized by congenital malformations of the great toes and progressive, debilitating heterotopic endochondral ossification (HEO) in characteristic anatomic patterns (axial > appendicular; dorsal > ventral; proximal > distal; cranial > caudal; upper limb > lower limb)( ). It is caused by PVs in ACVR1 ( ). No cases of malignancy have been documented in patients with FOP. However, patient and family education in line with other bone tumor syndromes is recommended. In addition, a new diagnosis of FOP should be considered when evaluating suspected “masses” in toes. Occipital Horn Syndrome Occipital Horn Syndrome (OHS) is a connective tissue disorder caused by PVs in ATP7A . This rare syndrome is characterized by connective tissue abnormalities, including hernias, joint laxity, cutis laxa and bladder diverticula. Downward pointing exostoses called “occipital horns” are a hallmark feature, and are located at the tendinous insertions of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles ( ). As with FOP and PSS, no cases of malignancy related to the degeneration of bony tumors have been reported, but patient and family education is again advised. Hereditary Leiomyomatosis and Renal Cell Cancer Syndrome Heterozygous germline PVs of fumarate hydratase ( FH ), encoding the enzyme catalyzing the conversion of fumarate to malate in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, cause hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer syndrome (HLRCC, OMIM #150800)( ). HLRCC is characterized by a predisposition to the development of benign cutaneous and uterine leiomyomata, and renal cell carcinoma (RCC)( – ). Homozygous FH PVs cause fumarase deficiency (FMRD; #606812)( ). To date, there have been no reports of leiomyomatosis and RCC occurring in FMRD, possibly reflecting the rarity of FMRD with only ~50 cases described to date, and the often short lifespan arising from the metabolic disorder( ). Furthermore, whilst family members/first-degree relatives of individuals with FMRD who are heterozygous for the FH variant are considered at increased risk of developing features associated with HLRCC, the most common germline FH PV causing FMRD, c.1431_1433dupAAA (p.Lys477dup), has been shown to be unassociated with an increased RCC risk( ). Among individuals affected by HLRCC, the age-related predisposition to uterine and cutaneous leiomyomata, whilst relying for the most part on symptomatic presentation, typically begins around the age of 20 years. However, the renal cancer risk has lifelong implications that do begin in childhood with calculated age-related penetrance of 1% by age 15y, 2% by age 20y, and 21% by age 70( , ). This is unlike some of the other RCC predisposition syndromes, such as Birt-Hogg-Dube Syndrome, in which the RCC risk begins in adulthood. Treatment of leiomyomata is warranted only for symptomatic lesions. Thus, we do not recommend surveillance for these lesions in childhood; however, education of female patients is important. Although infrequent, malignant transformation of cutaneous leiomyomata occurs in adults, and uterine leiomyomata rarely undergo this transformation( , – ). Therefore, carriers should be informed about rapid increase in growth rate or other concerning features of cutaneous lesions. To date, 15 children under 18 years of age have been reported in the literature with a diagnosis of RCC associated with HLRCC; these have all been reported in the second decade of life with a single case at age 7( , , ). Often, the RCC is symptomatic, leading to a new diagnosis of HLRCC, and it is important that the histological features of these RCC are recognized to enable accurate diagnosis. RCC associated with HLRCC reflects a distinct subtype with characteristic histology, including large nuclei and prominent nucleoli with perinucleolar clearing( , ). These features, together with the absence of the TFE3 translocation often seen in pediatric RCC, should raise suspicion of HLRCC-associated RCC. Although often not routinely available, immunohistochemical staining showing loss of fumarate hydratase expression with concomitant 2-succinyl-cysteine positivity is strongly indicative of an RCC that is HLRCC-associated( ). The RCC associated with HLRCC are typically aggressive and tend to have poor outcomes, often reflecting late-stage symptomatic presentations. In studies where renal imaging surveillance has been undertaken, RCCs have been detected, with patients alive at the time of reporting ( , ). Annual dedicated renal MRI surveillance is recommended for early RCC detection in HLRCC and we agree with the most recent international consensus recommendations suggesting that it should commence at around age 10 years( , ). MRI is preferred over ultrasound in view of the lower sensitivity of ultrasound for detecting HLRCC- associated RCC( ). The use of gadolinium-based contrast agents is preferred in some of the literature to enable accurate delineation of any cystic lesions that become complex in nature. However, concerns have been raised regarding gadolinium retention, and although no defined consequential clinical condition has been demonstrated, our consensus recommendation is to perform screening MRI scans without contrast but with diffusion-weighted imaging to aid detection of smaller lesions( ). If a renal lesion is detected on surveillance in the context of HLRCC, an MRI with contrast should be completed for characterization. In contrast to other hereditary RCC predisposition syndromes, prompt surgical resection with wide margins is indicated due to the aggressiveness of the RCC in this context, regardless of its size( ). Evaluation of RCC surveillance in HLRCC has found this to be both sensitive and specific, with no interval cancers being reported nor additional findings requiring invasive investigation( ). Annual renal MRI surveillance was found to be cost-effective when commencing at age 8 years, even with a low likelihood of RCC developing, reflecting RCC treatment costs and poor survival from symptomatic presentations( ). Given that FH catalyzes the step preceding that of succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) and SDHx PVs are associated with hereditary phaeochromocytoma-paraganglioma (HPP) syndrome( ), studies have sought to evaluate the incidence of Phaeochromocytoma (PHEO)/ Paraganglioma in HLRCC and whether specific FH PVs predispose to these neoplasms( ). PHEO/ Paraganglioma was described in 1% of an HLRCC cohort, and, recently, distinct FH variants predisposing to PHEO/ Paraganglioma were described( , , ). In the latter variant category, 22% of carriers developed PHEO/ Paraganglioma, while other FH genotypes demonstrated a prevalence of PHEO/ Paraganglioma of only 0.3–1.4%. The incidence of PHEO/Paraganglioma during childhood, for carriers of these specific variants, cannot be established given the paucity of reported cases to date, although it is likely very low. Nonetheless, it would seem that in the presence of a “PHEO/ Paraganglioma high risk” FH PVs, PHEO/ Paraganglioma surveillance is justified( ). Currently these FH variants are Thr234Ala and Cys434Tyr, while Ala194Thr, Leu303Ser and Asn329Ser are considered as likely pathogenic according to some (but not all) prediction tools. RCC risk might be lower in these variants, however, more studies are needed in order to determine the exact risk. Therefore, for these variants we recommend the same imaging surveillance for RCC in addition to surveillance for PHEO/ Paraganglioma. As per AACR recommendations for HPP (to be covered in an upcoming manuscript from the AACR Pediatric Cancer Working Group), surveillance should start at age 10 years and incorporate limited WBMRI covering the neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis (NCAP-WBMRI), including dedicated neck MRI, every 2 years for PHEO/ Paraganglioma. For RCC detection, NCAP-WBMRI will alternate with dedicated abdominal MRI, so that annual imaging of the kidneys is performed. In addition, annual measurements of both blood pressure and plasma/ urine fractionated metanephrines are recommended. Since SGS is extremely rare and most children have a short life span, knowledge of cancer in this condition is sparse and it is too early to implement genotype-phenotype correlations in advising approaches to management. Families should be made aware of the increased risk for tumors. Similar to the initial AACR recommendations for this condition( ), we again conclude that the merits of surveillance need to be weighed against the severity of the patient’s clinical condition. We recommend close attention to the presence of tumors on baseline diagnostic imaging and congenital anomalies in SGS. Thus, spine MRI is recommended as a baseline regarding the predilection of tumors for this region, and abdominopelvic ultrasound can also be considered. Germ cell and hepatoblastoma tumor markers (alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), beta human chorionic gonadotropin (bHCG), respectively) with other baseline syndrome-related bloodwork can be considered as well. For milder cases, clinicians may consider ongoing screening with spine MRI, periodic abdominal and pelvic ultrasound and periodic measurements of serum AFP and bHCG. Rubinstein-Taybi Syndrome Rubinstein–Taybi Syndrome (RSTS) is characterized by short stature, intellectual disability, broad thumbs and great toes and several facial features, including down-slanting palpebral fissures, high palate, low columella, grimacing smile and dental abnormalities( , ). RSTS is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner or de novo and the incidence is 1:100,000 to 1:125,000( , ). In 40%–50% of cases, RSTS is caused by germline PVs in CREBBP ( ) while the minority are caused by PVs in EP300 (3%–8% of cases)( ), both genes involved in a pathway that is also implicated in cancer( ). Various benign and malignant tumors have been described in individuals with RSTS. These case reports and small cohort studies have been reviewed by Boot et al., reporting a broad spectrum of 97 benign and malignant tumors in 89 individuals( ). In addition, they studied the incidence of neoplastic tumors in a nationwide cohort in the Netherlands of 87 individuals with RSTS. In comparison to the general Dutch population, the incidence of meningiomas and pilomatricomas was significantly elevated and they were the most frequent benign tumors. However, malignant tumors were not enriched, as only five were observed in four persons with RSTS (medulloblastoma; diffuse large-cell B-cell lymphoma; breast cancer; non-small cell lung carcinoma; colon carcinoma). Based on this cohort study, the authors conclude, similar to the advice in the 2017 AACR manuscript( ), that cancer surveillance recommendations are not indicated. Prompt assessment of any new or persistent symptoms is warranted.
